title: THEY CALLED HIM “CHRIST”—BUT MOST PEOPLE HAVE NEVER BEEN TOLD WHAT THAT WORD ACTUALLY MEANS
paragraphs:
THEY CALLED HIM “CHRIST”—BUT MOST PEOPLE HAVE NEVER BEEN TOLD WHAT THAT WORD ACTUALLY MEANS
“Messiah” is not Jesus’ last name. “Christ” is not merely a religious title. Behind both words is an ancient biblical reality of anointing, kingship, priesthood, suffering, victory, and a promise that reaches from Israel’s Scriptures all the way to the cross, the empty tomb, and the throne of God.
There is a moment in the Gospel of Matthew that is easy to read too quickly.
Jesus looks at His disciples and asks a question that eventually confronts every human heart:
“But whom say ye that I am?”
Peter answers:
“Thou art the Christ, the Son of the living God.”
—Matthew 16:15–16
We have heard those words so often that they can lose their force.
The Christ.
But what if you had been standing there in the first century?
What would you have heard?
Because Peter was not giving Jesus a surname.
He was making a staggering confession.
He was saying, in effect:
You are the One.
The promised King.
The Anointed One.
The One Israel has been waiting for.
The One upon whom everything ultimately turns.
And suddenly one of the most familiar words in Christianity becomes enormous.
“Christ” comes from the Greek word Χριστός—Christos—meaning “Anointed One.”
Behind that Greek title stands the Hebrew מָשִׁיחַ—māšîaḥ, commonly written “Messiah”—which likewise means “anointed one.”
That connection matters.
The English words “Messiah” and “Christ” may sound like two different religious concepts, but biblically they point to the same central idea.
The Messiah is the Christ.
The Christ is the Anointed One.
That is why John’s Gospel can say:
“We have found the Messias, which is, being interpreted, the Christ.”
—John 1:41
John even preserves the connection for his readers. The Greek text uses Μεσσίαν (Messian) and then explains it with Χριστός (Christos).
This was not decorative theology.
It was identity.
And to understand why that identity matters, you have to understand anointing.

In the Old Testament world, anointing could mark someone as specially appointed or consecrated for a God-given role. Kings were famously anointed. Priests were anointed. The language of anointing became inseparable from divine appointment, consecration, authority, and calling.
When Samuel anointed David, Scripture says:
“Then Samuel took the horn of oil, and anointed him in the midst of his brethren: and the Spirit of the LORD came upon David from that day forward.”
—1 Samuel 16:13
Imagine that scene.
David was not sitting on a throne.
He was not wearing a crown.
He was not commanding armies.
He was the overlooked son who had been out tending sheep.
Yet oil ran over the head of a shepherd boy while heaven declared something that circumstances had not caught up with yet.
A king was standing in the room.
That is one of the strange patterns of Scripture.
God's purposes are often present before human eyes recognize them.
David was anointed before he was enthroned.
And generations later, Israel was still waiting for David's greater Son.
The prophets had created an expectation that God would act decisively through His promised ruler.
Isaiah spoke of a coming figure upon whom God's Spirit would rest:
“And the spirit of the LORD shall rest upon him, the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and might, the spirit of knowledge and of the fear of the LORD.”
—Isaiah 11:2
Then Isaiah gives us another astonishing picture:
“The Spirit of the Lord GOD is upon me; because the LORD hath anointed me to preach good tidings unto the meek…”
—Isaiah 61:1
Centuries later, Jesus walked into a synagogue in Nazareth.
He was handed Isaiah.
He read:
“The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he hath anointed me to preach the gospel to the poor…”
Then He sat down.
Every eye was fixed on Him.
And Jesus said:
“This day is this scripture fulfilled in your ears.”
Think about the weight of that sentence.
Jesus was not merely announcing that He had an inspirational message.
He was placing Himself inside the fulfillment of Israel's prophetic hope.
The Anointed One had come.
But then the story becomes stranger.
Because if you were expecting God's Messiah to arrive, you might expect immediate visible conquest.
A throne.
An army.
Political liberation.
Public vindication.
Instead, the Messiah touches lepers.
He eats with people carrying terrible reputations.
He receives sinners.
He confronts hypocrisy.
He washes feet.
He weeps.
He allows Himself to be betrayed.
He is mocked.
Stripped.
Beaten.
And crucified.
That is where the scandal begins.
How could the Anointed King end up on a Roman cross?
How could the Messiah appear defeated?
How could the One who came announcing God's kingdom be hanging beneath an accusation written over His dying body?
The cross seemed to say that everything had gone wrong.
But the apostles came to proclaim something breathtaking:
The cross was not the cancellation of God's plan.
It stood at the very heart of God's saving purpose.
After His resurrection, Jesus told His disciples:
“Ought not Christ to have suffered these things, and to enter into his glory?”
—Luke 24:26
The Messiah who suffers before entering glory.
The King whose crown is preceded by thorns.
The victorious Christ whose triumph passes through death.
That changes the way we understand Jesus.
And it changes the way we understand grace.
Because Jesus was not anointed merely to become an inspirational figure you admire from a safe distance.
He came to save sinners.
That means people like us.
People with memories we wish we could erase.
People who have worshiped while hiding things.
People who promised God, “Never again,” and eventually did it again.
People who know the Bible but sometimes struggle to obey it.
People who have smiled at church while privately falling apart.
People who have carried guilt so long that shame started feeling like a name.
Maybe nobody knows your secret.
Maybe everyone thinks your faith is strong.
Maybe your Bible has highlighted verses while your heart has hidden rooms.
And perhaps the frightening question isn't whether other people would still love you if everything became visible.
Perhaps the question underneath it is:
Would Jesus still want me?
Look at the Gospel.
The answer is not that your sin does not matter.
It matters so much that Christ went to the cross.
The answer is that His grace is greater than your ability to save yourself.
Christianity does not tell sinners to pretend the darkness is light.
It calls us to repentance.
To confession.
To surrender.
To Christ.
And repentance is not paying God enough tears to persuade Him to become merciful.
Repentance turns from sin toward the God whose mercy has been revealed in Jesus Christ.
The Gospel destroys both our excuses and our despair.
You cannot stand at the cross and honestly say sin is insignificant.
But neither can a repentant sinner stand at the cross and honestly say there is no mercy for sinners.
The blood says otherwise.
Jesus said:
“For the Son of man is come to seek and to save that which was lost.”
—Luke 19:10
Lost.
That word may be more personal than some of us want to admit.
You can know worship songs and still wander.
You can post Bible verses and still be starving spiritually.
You can look clean in photographs and feel filthy in private.
You can know Christian language while slowly learning how to hide from the Christ whose name you speak.
Yet the Gospel keeps bringing us back to Him.
Not merely “Jesus the teacher.”
Not merely “Jesus the miracle worker.”
Not merely “Jesus who helps me accomplish my plans.”
Jesus the Christ.
The Messiah.
God's Anointed King.
The crucified and risen Lord.
This is why Peter's confession matters so deeply.
“Thou art the Christ.”
It is not trivia for a theology examination.
It demands a response.
If Jesus really is the Christ, then He is not an accessory to the life we have already decided to live.
We do not recruit the King into our plans.
We surrender to Him.
And this is where the meaning of “anointing” can become distorted in modern Christian culture.
Sometimes people speak about “the anointing” as though it were spiritual celebrity.
A powerful personality.
A platform.
A microphone.
An atmosphere.
A particular emotional sensation.
Or even a religious shortcut to prosperity and prominence.
But Scripture does not give us permission to reduce biblical anointing to charisma, fame, wealth, or human impressiveness.
Jesus—the Christ, the Anointed One—walked directly toward a cross.
His glory cannot be reduced to applause.
His kingdom cannot be reduced to branding.
His authority does not depend upon followers, views, stages, algorithms, or public approval.
And this matters for every Christian who has secretly wondered:
“If God is really with me, why is this so hard?”
Look at Christ.
Difficulty by itself does not prove abandonment by God.
Obedience can be costly.
Faithfulness can hurt.
Love can involve sacrifice.
Jesus' road to resurrection passed through Golgotha.
But be careful here.
The Gospel is not telling us that suffering saves us.
Jesus saves us.
Your pain does not atone for your sin.
Your tears do not purchase forgiveness.
Your religious performance cannot resurrect your soul.
Christ is the Savior.
That distinction is everything.
We do not need a motivational coach to teach dead hearts how to behave more successfully.
We need the living Christ.
And that is why another passage carries such power.
Peter preached:
“God anointed Jesus of Nazareth with the Holy Ghost and with power: who went about doing good, and healing all that were oppressed of the devil; for God was with him.”
—Acts 10:38
Then Peter does not stop with Jesus' ministry.
He moves to His death and resurrection.
Jesus was killed.
God raised Him.
The Gospel cannot be separated from the crucified and risen Christ.
That is the center.
And perhaps that is why this truth can feel uncomfortable.
Because if Jesus is merely inspirational, you can admire Him.
If Jesus is merely useful, you can call Him when life hurts.
If Jesus is merely a teacher, you can quote the teachings you like and quietly ignore the ones you don't.
But if Jesus is the Christ…
the King…
the Lord…
then eventually you have to decide what to do with His authority.
There are places inside us where we still want the crown.
Our money.
Our relationships.
Our sexuality.
Our ambitions.
Our grudges.
Our habits.
Our screens.
Our private thoughts.
Our reputation.
Our future.
We want Jesus close enough to rescue us but sometimes not close enough to rule us.
And He loves us too much to cooperate with that illusion.
Grace does not merely soothe.
Grace transforms.
Paul writes:
—2 Corinthians 5:17
Notice those words.
“In Christ.”
Not merely impressed by Christ.
Not culturally associated with Christ.
Not occasionally inspired by Christ.
In Christ.
The Anointed One becomes the center of a new identity.
This is where scandal becomes grace.
Peter himself is proof.
The man who declared, “Thou art the Christ,” later denied that he even knew Jesus.
Three times.
Think about the humiliation.
Peter had confessed the Messiah with his mouth and then, under pressure, denied Him with the same mouth.
If Peter's worst moment had been the final chapter, his story would have ended beside a charcoal fire with fear winning.
But Jesus writes endings differently.
After the resurrection, Peter encounters the risen Christ.
Failure is confronted.
Love is questioned.
Calling is restored.
“Feed my sheep.”
The man who denied Jesus became a witness to Jesus.
That is not permission to treat sin casually.
It is evidence that failure does not possess greater authority than the grace of the risen Christ.
Maybe that is the sentence somebody reading this needs tonight.
Your sin should bring you to repentance.
But your sin does not deserve the throne.
Jesus does.
Your shame does not deserve the throne.
Jesus does.
Your past does not deserve the throne.
Jesus does.
Your addiction does not deserve the throne.
Jesus does.
Your reputation does not deserve the throne.
Jesus does.
Your success does not deserve the throne either.
Jesus does.
He is the Christ.
And when that becomes more than vocabulary, Christianity stops being a religious decoration and becomes surrender.
Maybe you've spent years asking Jesus to bless a life you never actually surrendered to Him.
Maybe you know how to appear Christian.
Maybe nobody realizes how exhausted you are from maintaining the appearance.
You do not need another mask.
You need Christ.
Come into the light.
Confess what needs confessing.
Turn from what needs abandoning.
Make restitution where Scripture and wisdom require it.
Seek trustworthy Christian help where you need help.
Stop calling chains “personality.”
Stop calling compromise “just who I am.”
Stop treating tomorrow like a promise.
And do not confuse repentance with hopelessness.
You are not being invited to stare endlessly at yourself.
You are being called to look to Christ.
The Messiah has come.
The King was crucified.
The tomb is empty.
Jesus lives.
And sinners who come to Him do not need to manufacture a cleaner past before asking for mercy.
Scripture says:
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.”
—1 John 1:9
That is grace.
Not cheap grace.
Not pretend grace.
Blood-bought grace.
Grace that forgives.
Grace that cleanses.
Grace that teaches us to leave the darkness.
Grace that takes scandals human beings would use as permanent labels and refuses to let those labels have the final word over a repentant life surrendered to Christ.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
If this exposed something you have been hiding, don't manufacture a polished religious response.
Be honest.
If your spirit has felt dry and you need believers to stand with you in prayer, comment, “pray for me.”
Someone reading silently may desperately need evidence that grace still reaches people in real life.
And if one particular person came into your mind while reading this, don't ignore that.
Not to embarrass them.
Not to preach at them.
Because maybe they need to remember who Jesus really is.
Let your support become stewardship, not spiritual performance; gratitude, not guilt.
And whether or not you ever purchase anything, keep growing.
It means the Anointed One.
The promised King.
The Messiah.
But never confuse supporting Gospel Warrior with the Gospel itself.
We cannot sell grace.
No product can cleanse a conscience.
No ministry can replace Christ.
No platform died for you.
Jesus did.
Come to Christ.
The Messiah is not waiting for you to become impressive.
He calls sinners to repent and believe.
The King who wore the crown of thorns is risen.
And perhaps the scandal you thought would become the title of your life is only the place where grace is about to write a sentence you never thought possible.
Your darkest chapter does not get to name the book when the risen Christ holds the pen.
